findings.title: Working-hours end-time check uses slot start time instead of end time
findings.body: In checkIfIsAvailable's new working-hours validation, both `start` and `end` are computed from `slotStartTime` (`const end = slotStartTime.hour() * 60 + slotStartTime.minute();`). This means the check never actually validates whether the slot's end time exceeds the organizer's working hours — it only ever compares the start time against both boundaries. As a result, bookings that start within working hours but extend past the end of the working window will incorrectly be treated as 'within working hours' and remain bookable, defeating the purpose of this new safeguard.

findings.title: Dayjs objects compared with strict equality always evaluate false
findings.body: `dayjs(date.start).add(utcOffset, "minutes") === dayjs(date.end).add(utcOffset, "minutes")` compares two freshly constructed Dayjs object instances by reference. Since dayjs() always returns a new object, this condition can never be true, even when start and end actually represent the same instant. The intended special-case handling for zero-duration (point-in-time) date overrides is therefore dead code and will never trigger.

findings.title: Date override lookup only inspects the first matching override per day
findings.body: `dateOverrides.find(...)` stops at the first override entry whose date matches the slot's date and makes the availability decision based solely on that entry, setting `dateOverrideExist = true` as a side effect inside the callback. If a schedule has multiple override time ranges for the same date (which Cal.com's UI allows, e.g. split availability on one date), only the first range in array order is evaluated; subsequent ranges for that date are silently ignored, which can incorrectly mark a slot as unavailable (or available) when a later override entry for the same date would have produced a different result.

findings.title: Timezone offset calculation depends on server's local timezone via Date.toString()
findings.body: `dayjs(override.start.toString()).tz(override.timeZone).utcOffset()` and the analogous invitee line convert the Date to a string via `Date.prototype.toString()` before re-parsing with dayjs. `toString()` renders the date using the host process's system timezone, so the resulting calendar date fed into `.tz()` can shift depending on where the Node process runs (and can roll over to an adjacent day near local midnight). This makes the organizer/invitee UTC-offset difference used for date-override conversion non-deterministic across deployment environments, instead of being based purely on the override's actual UTC instant.

findings.title: Duplicated, divergently-implemented date-override timezone logic
findings.body: Date-override timezone adjustment is now implemented twice with different math: once here (DST-diff based, using `dayjs().tz(...).utcOffset() - startOfInviteeDay.tz(...).utcOffset()`), and separately in packages/trpc/server/routers/viewer/slots.ts's checkIfIsAvailable (plain `utcOffset()` diff with no DST adjustment). Because both paths independently decide whether an override applies/at what time, and they can diverge (e.g., around DST transitions), the two filters can disagree on the same slot, making the overall availability result inconsistent and harder to reason about or fix in only one place.

findings.title: No test coverage for the headline round-robin fixed-host date-override fix
findings.body: The PR description states its main purpose is fixing that fixed-host date overrides are respected for round-robin events (Fixes #8207), with explicit manual test steps involving a round-robin event with a fixed host and a round-robin host. However, the only test added in this file extends the existing single-user 'Check for Date overrides' test with a different invitee timezone; there is no new test exercising a ROUND_ROBIN event type with a fixed host plus override, nor verifying that round-robin host overrides don't block availability while fixed-host overrides do. This leaves the primary bug fix unverified by automated tests.
